idiom_name: dict of topic -> list of callables, dispatched over a snapshot, with weakref.WeakMethod/WeakSet
implementation_notes: Python's standard library has no broadcast facility, so the channel is a registry the application writes: a dict from event type or name to a list of callables, publish iterating over a copy of the list, and subscribe returning a callable that removes the entry. Storing bound methods strongly keeps their owners alive, so use weakref.WeakMethod (or a WeakSet of listeners) when the subscriber's lifetime is independent of the bus; a queue or asyncio fan-out is the asynchronous variant of the same structure. The registry is small but it is application code with application bugs, which is why many projects take the blinker dependency instead.
pitfalls: Iterating the live list while a handler unsubscribes skips or repeats handlers - always dispatch over a snapshot.
Strong references to bound methods and closures keep owners (and their exception tracebacks) alive: use weakref.WeakMethod/WeakSet or unsubscribe on teardown.
Publishing from several threads without a lock races with list mutation; the GIL does not make the registry update atomic.

variants.name: blinker named signals
variants.implementation_notes: blinker is the de-facto Python signal bus for library code: signal('name') returns a process-global named signal, connect() registers receivers (weak by default) and send() notifies all of them and collects their return values, while connect_via() narrows a receiver to one sender and muted() disables a signal in tests. It removes the registry boilerplate and the weak-reference trap at the cost of a global namespace of signal names and one extra dependency; Flask's signals are built on it.
pitfalls: Sends are synchronous and in connection order; an exception in one receiver aborts notification of the rest.
Named signals are process-global, so unrelated libraries can share a name by accident - namespace signal names after the owning module.
Sending with no receivers is cheap but silently does nothing; tests that expect a consumer should assert on the receivers property.
